title: How Anti-Corruption Politics Destroyed Brazil
author: Alex Hochuli
content:
![How Anti-Corruption Politics Destroyed
Brazil](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/10/AP26256634675540.jpg)

Brazil 's upcoming election pits President Lula da Silva, eighty, against
Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, forty-five. If he wins, Lula will serve a record
fourth (non-consecutive) term. His opponent is the son of former president
Jair Bolsonaro. To much of the unenthusiastic electorate, it feels like an
election about nothing. Both candidates have rejection rates between 45 and 55
percent. Lula's slogan is "Brazil, ready for more" (of what?); Flavio mainly
wants to get his dad out of jail. It is the old versus the not-quite-new.

> "No one really rules Brazil."

That isn't to say that matters of great importance won't be decided. The
issues at stake include the growing national debt, who has access to rare
earth minerals, and a slew of soon-vacant seats on the Supreme Court. The
problem, however, is that no one really rules Brazil. After a decade defined
by an unending string of scandals, the country suffers a crisis of legitimacy
and a void of political authority.

Lula's Workers Party (PT) has held the presidency for seventeen of the past
twenty-four years. But with a small minority of seats in Congress, the party
has proven unable to impose a governing program in the way holding office
would suggest. The Bolsonaro clan still has leadership of the conservative
camp, having supplanted the moderate center-right eight years ago in a
radicalization similar to that which took place across Western Europe or North
America. But Jair Bolsonaro is imprisoned and unhealthy, and his sons inspire
little loyalty beyond the base. Their response to the impasse has been to look
up for salvation--to North America and Donald Trump.

On the issues that pollsters say most concern Brazilians--security, above all,
but also the cost of living, health and education--there is little concrete
debate, let alone vision. Instead, Brazil is riven by scandal and institutions
at each other's throats. Most notable is the Supreme Court. Justices launch
accusations at colleagues in public sessions while Congress threatens to
impeach them. It is comeuppance for an institution that has become far too
powerful, and in particular for one judge who made himself sovereign: Supreme
Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes.

At the center of the latest scandal is Daniel Vorcaro, a disgraced banker
responsible for the country's largest ever banking fraud and a much less-
discussed scheme for legally ripping off public workers through a payroll-
deduction credit card. In only a few years, Vorcaro became incredibly well-
connected, benefiting from the benign neglect of the Central Bank president
and paying off other directors at the institution. He hosted bunga-bunga
parties in New York for Brazil's financial and political elite and traveled on
one of his multiple private jets to Courchevel with his "friend for life," an
influential senator to whom he was paying monthly stipends of between $60,000
and $95,000. The scandal around Vorcaro's defunct Banco Master revealed a
compromised regulator, a drained state bank, bought-off politicians, a prison
suicide, plunder of public funds, and a very bad bit of cinema.

Of greatest consequence are Vorcaro's links to Supreme Court justices. He
hosted them at lavish dinners, went into business with one, hired the spouses
of others as lawyers for exorbitant fees, and in general held contacts that a
sober judge should judge untoward. We know all of this because institutional
politics in Brazil is now conducted through that most contemporary and
mercurial of means: leaks, especially of private communications. And in Brazil
that means WhatsApp.

To take one example: Two days before Vorcaro was sensationally arrested at the
airport as he tried to flee to Dubai, he messaged Moraes, "does [Central Bank
President] Galipolo know? By Monday do I need to be gone?" Other messages
retrieved from Vorcaro's phone signal his life-long gratitude to Moraes. The
messages were written in the iPhone Notes app, screenshotted, and sent as one-
time view messages, a mode of communication Moraes himself had classified as
an obstruction of justice in another case. Moraes's phone was not seized,
meaning his replies are unknown and the justice's complicity is unproven. But
the stain of scandal remains.

It is less clear who benefits electorally from Vorcaro's fall. In 2025, Moraes
sentenced Jair Bolsonaro to twenty-seven years imprisonment for an
incompetently attempted coup in early 2023; the judge had also been running an
almost autonomous, wide-ranging inquiry into "fake news" that saw him
summarily take social media accounts off air, leading to a spectacular clash
with Elon Musk. All of this allowed him to cast himself as the guarantor of
Brazilian democracy (of a bulletproofed, not-very-representative sort). As
such, he has become associated with the institutional left, with the PT, and
with Lula.

The scandal around him should therefore help Flavio: Who wouldn't desire the
destruction of his father's jailer? But dig deeper and there are always
further complications. Another justice, Dias Toffoli, is even more implicated
with Vorcaro and Banco Master, but he was not investigated and his
communications not leaked, because the justice who holds rapporteurship, Andre
Mendonça, is a Bolsonaro appointee. Two weeks ago it came to a head in a
degrading spectacle, with justices calling each other liars. Brazilians now
once again know the names and faces of those they maybe shouldn't--those who
should be quiet and demure upholders of the Constitution.

* * *

Does anyone care? According to pollster
[_Datafolha_](https://datafolha.folha.uol.com.br/opiniao-e-
sociedade/2026/09/falta-de-confianca-no-stf-supera-partidos-e-congresso-e-e-a-
mais-alta-ja-registrada.shtml?ref=compactmag.com), nearly half the population
feel the Supreme Court and Master scandal will influence their vote, with over
a third saying it will have a big influence. Flavio voters care more than Lula
voters (by 45 to 26 percent), and greater numbers think the left is more
implicated than the right.

If the scandal helps to put an end to Lula's political career, it would be the
most ironic, and bathetic, of denouements. Since 2014, Brazil has undergone a
series of rolling crises, centered around corruption revelations. These crises
intersect with--they are both cause and consequence of--economic downturns and
strangling institutional dysfunction.

In 2014, the _Lava Jato_ corruption probe revealed an arachnoid scheme of
overbilling and kickbacks between the state-controlled oil giant Petrobras,
huge construction companies, and multiple political parties. Running until
2021, it led to the arrest of business leaders and sitting politicians
including Lula himself, who spent 580 days in jail. The revelations served as
political fuel, but not legal justification, for impeaching Lula's successor,
Dilma Rousseff, in 2016. The first irony is that it was the PT who had first
empowered the judiciary and the public prosecutor to carry out the relevant
investigations. Then a radical section of the judiciary, wedded to highly
legalistic conception of society, pursued Lula for years.

The second ironic reversal was the revelation in 2019 that the anti-corruption
campaign was itself corrupted. A series of leaks revealed the judge and the
prosecutor were in cahoots, with the lead judge back-seat driving
investigations and orchestrating leaks to the media, whose reporting was
sometimes even used as corroborating evidence. Lula was released, and his and
many others' convictions were annulled.

When former army captain Jair Bolsonaro was elected on a wave of anti-
political sentiment, he hired Lula's jailer as his justice minister. The
latter quit after a year under a cloud of disgrace and his own discomfort at
being used. Bolsonaro's _disgovernment_ was characterized by institutional
chaos amidst the pandemic, as he set out to deliberately impede governmental
capacities. Pursuing re-election, he turned on the fiscal firehose--a "secret
budget" of congressional amendments that would ultimately total some $10
billion by the end of 2022, equivalent to a quarter of discretionary fiscal
spending. It became part of a process by which the legislature would become
ever more powerful, hoovering up pork for itself.

Lula returned, promising to save democracy. As if to prove the point,
_Bolsonaristas_ caused chaos in order to prompt the military to intervene.
They also cooked up a scheme to assassinate Lula along with Justice Alexandre
de Moraes, who would take on the rapporteurship of the coup-attempt case.

Moraes--known as _Xand ao_ (in English it would be "Big Lex")--had always been
associated with the center-right. But in another one of these strange
reversals of political polarity that mark our age, Moraes became a hero to the
left: scourge of coup mongers, jailer of Bolsonaro, and in the clash with Elon
Musk over social media takedown orders, defender of national sovereignty
against the Trump-aligned magnate. Moraes was even placed under sanctions by
the Trump administration.

For the left, the myth of the impartial judge had been buried in the febrile
atmosphere of the right-wing anti-corruption crusade of the mid-2010s.
Moraes's pursuit of _Bolsonaristas_ did the same for the far right, which in
turn re-enchanted the left with the counter-majoritarian power of the togas
and the courts. It would be yet another irony if _Xand ao_'s implication in
the Master scandal gives Flavio Bolsonaro the narrow edge to put an end to
Lula's political career.

> "Now it is the Supreme Court in the crosshairs."

Forty-five percent of Brazilians now distrust the Supreme Court, the highest
on record. It is about the same level as for Congress, political parties, and
the presidency. These latter numbers are actually down on the historic levels
of distrust--indeed, disgust--that they hit last decade, when they reached the
high sixties. But it is not so much that these institutions have recuperated
any of their legitimacy as that the spectacle of scandal has moved on. Now it
is the Supreme Court in the crosshairs.

This is the institutional razed earth of the anti-corruption crusade, its long
hangover. If we understand politics as the union of ideals and interests,
concretized in a program, and advanced by representatives of the people, then
this whole practice has come to be undermined, degraded. _Lava Jato_ presented
itself as a noble attempt to put an end to corruption once and for all but,
behind this moralistic ideal, there was a great deal of cynicism about any
national project for Brazil and the grubby compromises that always accompany
capitalist politics. The radical judiciary believed that no progress could be
made until Brazil was set on its proper legal footing. That puts the cart
before the horse. The history of development around the world shows that there
is no order before progress.

Instead of enabling progress, moralistic fervor and resigned disappointment
have lowered expectations. Scandal-mongering has become the central tool of
politics, wielded first by the right, then by the left, and now by the right
again. Indeed, the left now keeps trying to pin Vorcaro on the right. It has
some basis for doing so: Vorcaro made hundred-million dollar payments to fund
a (still-unmade) hagiographic [_film_](https://artreview.com/dark-horse-the-
bolsonaro-biopic-you-have-to-see-to-believe-opinion-euan-
marshall/?ref=compactmag.com) about Jair Bolsonaro; the suspicion is that this
was to cover living costs for Flavio's brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, self-exiled
in the United States after being sentenced for lobbying against his own
country.

At every turn, politics becomes further demoralized. Congress has become fat
on pork but has no desire to lead. Having suffered the scare of _Lava Jato_ ,
during which one-sixth of legislators were under investigation, congressmen
aspire to little more than remaining in office. Meanwhile, over 90 percent of
the federal budget goes on mandatory spending and the share remaining to the
president is shrinking fast. The executive cannot really lead, and government
can only be accomplished by diving into the swamp.

The upper ranks of the judiciary sought to fill this vacuum of authority, but
every activist step it took in attempting to right the republic undermined its
role as guarantor of the constitution. Who elected them anyway? So it is
perhaps fitting that Brazil's latest leak-lubricated scandal has come for the
judiciary.

Whoever wins October's election will not really [_rule
Brazil_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2GJJLMnJ8pw&ref=compactmag.com).
Lula's workout videos do not disguise a loss of political vigor. He does not
feel like a man in tune with his times, and he has no credible successor. But
if Lula can't lead, Flavio doesn't want to. His clan's imbrication with
organized crime and subservience to Washington tells you all you need to know
about their ultimate ambitions. Finance, agribusiness, and the extractive
industries will win again.
